content: A metered-dose inhaler (MDI) is a medical device designed to deliver a precise amount of medication directly to the lungs. It is commonly prescribed for managing conditions such as asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), and other respiratory disorders. MDIs are classified as aerosolized devices due to their method of medication delivery. The inhaler is composed of two primary components: the canister and the mouthpiece. The canister contains a metering dose valve with an actuating stem, and inside it, there is a mixture of the aerosol propellant and the medication. The mouthpiece includes a discharge nozzle that aligns with the canister and is typically equipped with a dust cap to prevent contamination. To use the inhaler, the patient presses down on the top of the canister while supporting the mouthpiece with their thumb. This action releases a fine mist of medication, which the patient inhales into their lungs. The medications delivered via MDIs are most commonly bronchodilators, corticosteroids, or a combination of the two. Less frequently, MDIs may be used to administer mast cell stabilizers, such as cromoglicate or nedocromil. One of the key advantages of MDIs is their rapid onset of action. For example, short-acting bronchodilators, often referred to as quick-relief medications, typically begin to work within five to 15 minutes when inhaled. In contrast, oral asthma medications may take one to three hours to take effect. For both adults and children, the use of a holding chamber or spacer device can make the administration of medication easier and more effective. However, it is important to note that the availability of MDIs approved for pediatric use in the United States is subject to ongoing changes by the FDA. Spacers are attachments that connect to the inhaler and act as a reservoir or holding chamber for the medication. When used correctly, spacers can improve the effectiveness of an inhaler by up to 20%. Spacers are particularly beneficial for individuals, including children and adults, who may have difficulty using a standard inhaler. For patients using corticosteroid inhalers, spacers are especially recommended to prevent the medication from depositing in the mouth, which can lead to oral yeast infections. Each metered-dose inhaler is designed to deliver a specific number of doses, which is indicated on the canister. While the inhaler may continue to function beyond the specified number of uses, the amount of medication delivered per puff may no longer be accurate. It is essential to keep track of the number of doses used and replace the inhaler once the recommended number of uses has been reached. Some manufacturers, such as those producing Ventolin and Advair, have addressed this issue by incorporating dose counters into the mouthpiece. Depending on the manufacturer, inhalers may be sold as a complete unit or as a refillable canister that can be replaced with a prescription. In the United States, metered-dose inhalers previously used chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) as a propellant to deliver medication. However, under the 1987 Montreal Protocol on Substances that Deplete the Ozone Layer, the use of CFCs in inhalers has been phased out. As of December 2008, all CFC-containing inhalers have been discontinued and replaced with hydrofluoroalkane-pressurized metered-dose inhalers (HFA pMDIs), which are more environmentally friendly.
